Hello there! I am a game designer and programmer with an artistic background in Illustration and shading.
Lantern of SoulsLearn about my custom camera manager and player controls.Explore GamePowerPlantLearn about my completely solo project.Explore GameBonevoyageLearn about my camera and dialogue system.Explore GameCupid ShooterLearn about my system for managing couples.Explore Game

What does our camera do?#Lantern of Souls is our current senior capstone, and I was tasked with designing the custom camera manager that fit our needs. Our camera is a dynamic 3rd person camera with our player on the third, and his soul to his side. The camera needed to be able to handle:
Smoothly springarming against walls but not smaller objects switching between our dynamic camera to fixed cameras swtiching to first person within cracks, and allowing the player to look around smoothly switching to cinematics such as dramatic quick time events Design of Springarm#The purpose of our spring arm is to prevent the camera from clipping through walls, pushing the camera closer or towards the center. It currently uses three line traces: one from the player’s head to the camera, one from the camera to straight down, and one from the player to the right vector.
The ray shooting from the head will push the camera to the ray’s collision point, but the ray shooting right from the player will push the camera to the center of the player if it colides.
Code BreakdownThe linetrace collision for the springarm is divided into 3 parts. The first linetrace is to see the location of the wall hit. The trace starts above the players head. this is done by getting the actor location and adding (15, 0, 150) to move it above the players head The trace ends 300 centimeters behind the player by subtracting (300, -90, -35) to the actor location and plugging that into the end.
The outhit location is then used to make a new camera offset. I get the actor location, subtracted that by the outhit location to get the length, I then subtract it by 12,12,12 to make the location land before the wall. (if you get the exact location the camera clips through). I unrotate the vector and that is our new desired camera offset.
The second linetrace shoots down from where the camera normally would be without collision, and that sees if there is a floor. If there isn’t a floor, it spring arms. This method is planned to change in the future when we implement tags.
The third linetrace shoots off to the right to prevent the camera from clipping to the right side of a wall. When the line collides, it brings the camera to the center of the player.
Camera States#My camera switches on an enum between various states such as Looking, Fixed Camera, Peek left, Peek Right, Crack Look, and a death cutscene similar to fixed camera. This system has been easy for my team to follow along and adjust elements if needs be.
LookingNormal Looking is how the looking camera typically works. The desired camera offset changes continuously depending on collisions with walls. If the desired camera offset is different from the actual camera offset, the actual offset will lerp to the desired camera offset.This accounts for changes with wall collisions
Lerp into normal looking is how the looking camera works if we need to interpolate into the looking camera. This happens if we need to transition from another camera mode like Fixed Camera.
FixedThis is a camera that stays in a set position. You can choose to lerp to it or not. Typically used for interactables or cutscenes.
It takes in an arrow within interactables and sets that to the desired camera location and rotation.
Above is a function that my team are able to easily call and plug in an arrow any time they make a new interactable. They are also able to decide if they want to lerp to the camera or cut to the camera.
Peek Left/ Peek RightPeek left and peek right shift the camera to either side and allows the player to look around corners. This adds to the stealth a player can utilize. Q allows the player to peek to the left, and E allows the player to peek to the right. Those inputs are handled in the game controller. Peek left and peek right simply lerp the actual camera offset to a position that is off to the side. It takes the current desired camera location and adds to the Y for peek left and subtracts for peek right. If there is a wall collision that is detected in the Camera orient however, it will interpolate off to the side of the collision location.
Crack LookCrack look started off as a fixed camera that would just switch to peek left and right, which were more fixed cameras. However we wanted the experience in the crack to be more interactive. This is first done by letting the player look around the crack with their mouse.
Then with the quick time event, we wanted something dynamic, which the camera movements had to match. The player is able to look around the corners with the mouse, when the enemy is around the area, and decides to look inside the crack, a quick time event starts.
